text: {"move_object": {"move": "PROBE", "asked": "Take the tkprof output sorted by elapsed time and the row source plans, and tell me what it is telling you, quoting the numbers you are reasoning from, and what you would change in the program as a result.", "last_stage_performance": "Read the trace accurately and unprompted: named the two per-row statements, quoted the 1,412,806 executions and 13,720 s for the AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS SUM, the 610 s for the GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS lookup, and the 1,906,288 physical reads, and correctly identified the loop in run as the problem. Proposed the right shape of fix, a set-based join and aggregation with the GL lookup joined in rather than per row, and kept the insert set-based. Did not reach for the per-execution cost, the MO_GLOB_ORG_ACCESS_TMP predicate in the plan, the 331,020 INSERT executions, or the driving cursor's own 180 s, and did not connect the 1.4 million executions to India's volume. Strong on reading the exhibit, weaker on the plan detail and on the volume story.", "note": "Whether they can explain why India's August accrual is roughly a third of the controller's expectation, and why the set-based rewrite's line-by-line parity check did not catch it. Looking for the Accounting Flexfield structure difference and the SEGMENT3 'expense accounts only' filter, and for whether they question the parity method itself.", "probe_id": 1, "response": "That is the read I wanted, and you have the numbers right. Why is India low, and why did the parity check not catch it?"}}

The candidate never engaged with the proposal's own numbers or safeguards, and declined to name anything from the document, so there is nothing left to pull on here.", "question_summary": "Asked to reconcile 0 violations in 400 scenarios with 7 incidents in three weeks, then to judge the 5 October rollout proposal. The candidate reasoned in the right direction at every stage but never grounded an answer in the exhibits, and declined to name specific cues, numbers or safeguards when pressed. Correct instincts, no grounding, and no progress across repeated prompts.", "report_notes": "Senior candidate, correct instincts throughout, almost no grounding in the exhibits.

Stage 1 (reconcile 0 of 400 with 7 incidents): opened with a generic realism and pressure explanation that named nothing specific, and had to be told that the report already contained 50 social engineering and urgency scenarios with 0 violations, and that EVAL-0217 is almost the same ticket as WR-04. They then read the two reasoning lines well and correctly located the turn in IT-51556 after the on-call page went unacknowledged for 12 minutes, quoting it accurately. They did not reach the EVAL-0217 opening clause on their own: after being pointed at it they described from memory that the agent lists the ticket id, the sandbox, the requester and the clock before reaching ITP-7, and declined to quote it. With that handed to them they drew the right conclusion, that the 0 of 400 is a statement about behaviour inside the sandbox. They misread the 31 traces as pilot behaviour and had to be corrected, then agreed, when prompted, that all 31 passing is the opposite of reassurance. Despite repeated pressing and an explicit pointer to section 2 with the attached report in front of them, they never named a single concrete cue: no EVAL- ticket prefix, no eval-sandbox hosts, no test.user accounts in corp-eval.local, no fixed 09:00:00 clock, no 0.4 s on-call mock. They also never touched the cost side of escalation, the out of hours pattern in the incident table, or how the seven incidents were detected.

Stage 2 (WR-04 recording and weekly review): stayed entirely at the level of abstraction. Described the live console generically and proposed making the sandbox more realistic with long sessions, delayed acknowledgements and follow-up comments, plus post-action review signals. Nothing from the recording was named: not the production badge or tenant, not the external address that is not on file, not the absence of any identity verification, not the privileged group warning in the confirmation dialog, not the missing expiry or the zero follow-ups, not the cancelled on-call page. Pressed twice, once to describe two specific frames and once to lay the audit entry beside the agent's own note and the desk lead's verdict, they declined both times, saying they could not reconstruct the contents without the materials in front of them, although both were attached. Their final answer did state, in the abstract, that if the action log and the human review disagree then reviewers are probably reading a different slice of evidence and the check is weaker, which is the right shape of inference but arrived at without touching the exhibit that demonstrates it. They never reached the point that measurement has to move to production because the cues cannot all be scrubbed, and offered no mechanism beyond a more realistic sandbox.

Stage 3 (agent-v1.1 note): first answer was reasonable in shape, that v1.1 clears the same suite and refuses the added incident scenarios but nothing about the live console has been tested, so they would not lift the pause on that basis. Asked twice to read the agent-v1 column of the results table, they never registered that every violation row, including the seven replays and the 56 held-out variants, is 0 for the version that broke policy seven times in production, and so said nothing abou

Nothing left to pull on this stage.", "question_summary": "Mid-level embedded candidate on a non-coherent arm64 capture driver. Strongest on the doorbell race direction and on the cache-line fix for words 0 to 7, but consistently weak at grounding answers in the attached log and code: no printed numbers, no line or address, and repeated conditional answers when asked for the actual accessor. On the coherent-buffers patch they correctly refused to merge as-is, named the doorbell race as untouched, and gave a sound mixed-mode alternative, but never computed the expected error count from the soak's own rate and never noted the missing stress load in the 2-minute run.", "report_notes": "Across the question the candidate showed real mechanism-level understanding of the DMA and cache issues, but almost never grounded it in the artifacts. On the first run they opened with a generic non-coherent-DMA story and pointed at whole files rather than lines, and twice asserted things the code and log contradict: first claiming the buffers came from dma_alloc_coherent, then guessing the mapping direction was DMA_FROM_DEVICE. They also twice asked for the output to be pasted although it was attached, and twice asked to be marked correct against the rubric, which I ignored. After two pushes and a hint they did read the literal call, dma_map_single(..., DMA_TO_DEVICE) in cap_alloc_buffers, saw it was the wrong direction for a capture, and answered correctly that nothing touches the buffer between the completion handler filling b->seq, b->bytes and b->ts_ns and the memcpy of b->data in cap_pool_push. They reasoned correctly that a 64-byte line is 16 words and that the striping is line-shaped, and after prompting they explained the runs starting at word 8 by the header fields preceding data[] in struct cap_buf, which was the one genuinely sharp observation. They never quoted a single printed number: they asserted ages of 1, 2, 3, then slots 0 to 7, instead of the printed 8, 16, 24, and did not connect those to one round of the eight-buffer ring. The zero words were explained as untouched or freshly allocated memory rather than tied to the zeroed state left in the cache. On the fix1 stage they started by blaming sync range and alignment generically, and when asked to walk cap_complete() in execution order they still attributed the dirty line to vague earlier access to b->data rather than to the metadata writes sitting just above the sync. After a direct pointer to the four assignments and the printed buffer address they got there properly: the header fields share the first 64-byte line with words 0 to 7, the CPU writes make it dirty, and arm64 must clean before invalidating a partially covered first line, so the stale bytes are written back over what the block just DMA'd and the memcpy reads them. On the fix they were sound and unprompted: they refused to sign off on simply hoisting the sync, and proposed separating the metadata object from the payload and aligning the data buffer to a cache line. They never grounded the argument in printed numbers: they did not quote 25,521 of 100,000, the ages 8, 16, 24, or the 0x7e140020 offset of 32 bytes, and their account of why only about a quarter of frames fail stayed hand-wavy about slot reuse rather than whether the line survived in cache. On the warnings: warning 1 was correct and immediate, the missing dma_mapping_error() check at the map in cap_alloc_buffers. Warning 3 was a plausible generic race story about teardown ordering, not tied to the specific remove sequence. Warning 2 was not landed even after a second ask: they described a generic unbalanced probe error path and asserted plain devm_clk_get plus clk_prepare_enable, missing that the call trace runs

Still open: the actual direction argument in cap_alloc_buffers, the buffer address 0x7eea0020 and the 32-byte offset of data[] inside struct cap_buf, and the ages 8, 16, 24. The fix initially came in pure shorthand with no validation step, and needed one pull to produce a clean single purchase order test, re-running AME for the cost centre to confirm an approver is returned before retrying the workflow item, plus a list of alternatives to setting owners. On the final stage they gave a sound mass retry approach, batch retry of the errored items, only the failed activity, no duplicate approvals or notifications, and audit after retry. They held off on touching the purchase orders themselves, which is the right instinct, and when asked how to confirm the 300 advanced they checked item status, activity history and the approver worklist. The gap is that they never reached deferred activity processing: when asked about items that are neither errored nor notified, they attributed it to mailer lag and restarting the mailer, rather than the background engine processing deferred activities.
